references.text: The serpent is introduced as the most cunning of all the beasts of the field – the background for the curse pronounced in v.14.
The Lord pronounces a curse on Adam as a consequence of the fall, which mirrors the curse on the serpent.
In the new creation, the serpent will still eat dust, an allusion to the curse in Gen 3:14 that persists even in the renewed world.
Peoples shall lick the dust like the serpent – a direct allusion to the serpent's curse to eat dust all the days of its life.
Jesus is described as the one who, through his death, breaks the devil's power, which can be seen in connection with the judgment on the serpent.
The ancient serpent is identified with the devil and Satan and cast down to earth – providing background for understanding the serpent in Gen 3.
Satan, referred to as the ancient serpent, is bound – an eschatological fulfillment of the judgment on the serpent in Gen 3:14.
No more curse shall exist – the final removal of the curse that began with the judgment in Eden's garden.
The NT reveals the spiritual identity (the devil) behind the serpent in Genesis, and links the judgment to the devil's ultimate defeat.
